newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans to slash crude imports into summer.
newsitem.headline: Romania plans to slash crude imports into summer.

text.p: Romania will slash crude oil imports to nearly half current levels within months in view of lower summer demand and government moves to restructure the refining sector, an oil industry official said on Wednesday.
"This month, we imported 750,000 tonnes of crude and in May the figure should be 650,000 tonnes," an official from the main oil trader Petrolexportimport SA said by telephone.
"Of April's imports, 50 percent came from Russia and the rest from Egypt, Iran as well as from Iraq within the oil-for-food arrangement approved by the United Nations."
He said lower demand and the government decision to close down two of the country's 11 refineries would push imports down to 400,000 tonnes through the summer months.
"We must take into account the moves planned by the government and adjust our imports accordingly," he said.
Last week, the government put the big Black Sea coast Petromidia refinery and the Darmanesti refinery in eastern Romania, on a list of loss-making firms earmarked for closure.
Data show Petromidia's losses amounted to almost five percent from the losses recorded by Romania's economy in 1996.
The proposed closures are part of an ambitious programme launched by the new centrist government to fill the black holes which have siphoned off huge funds.
The Balkan country has a refining capacity of 34 million tonnes a year, built up by late Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, which far exceeds its needs.
The Petrolexportimport official said his company had yet to decide on the arrangements for the future crude imports.
"We still have to decide whether to conclude contracts now or buy the crude on the spot market later on," he said.
Petrolexportimport, which last year was confronted with problems related to late payments, was "very liquid" and able to pay in time, the official said. There were no outstanding bills.
Last year, lack of funds and a shortage of hard currency on the country's interbank market forced the state-run company to renegotiate some of its payment deadlines.
But Petrolexportimport managed to solve the problems in January, when it signed an accord with Chase Manhattan Corp for a $200 million revolving credit, guaranteed by the government.
"The process of paying back the loan to Chase is going on smoothly," the official also said.
